text: Let's write actual Python. We'll start with the most basic building block: variables, and the handful of types you'll use constantly.

No declaration keyword, no explicit type required — you just assign. model_name = "gpt-4o" becomes a string because of the quotes. max_tokens = 500 becomes an integer. Python infers the type from the value — that's dynamic typing.

Five types you'll see constantly: str for text, int for whole numbers, float for decimals, bool for True or False, and None — Python's explicit way of saying 'no value yet,' different from zero or an empty string.

type() tells you what type a value actually is. Python won't silently combine incompatible types — "5" + 3 raises an error instead of a surprise. You convert explicitly: int("25") turns text into a number.
The standard way to build text from variables is an f-string: f before the opening quote, curly braces around any variable inside. You'll use this constantly for prompts, logs, and error messages.
Variables and types are the foundation everything else sits on. Next up: control flow — teaching your code to make decisions and repeat itself with if, for, and while.
